name: Reliance Global Group, Inc.

profile.description: Reliance Global Group is a micro-cap InsurTech company headquartered in Lakewood, New Jersey, that acquires and operates wholesale and retail insurance agencies under its RELI Exchange brand and the direct-to-consumer 5MinuteInsure.com platform. CEO Ezra Beyman is repositioning the company as an 'AI-native' insurance platform, having hired a CTO from Coinbase/Capital One in June 2026 and launched an AI agent for back-office automation. The company executed a 1-for-40 reverse stock split in May 2026 to regain Nasdaq compliance and has since seen the stock recover to ~$2.50, though consolidated commission income continues to decline following divestitures of non-core agencies, with TTM revenue of $11.0M and a $4.2M market cap.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Health insurance policies written through RELI Exchange grew 72% YoY during the 2025 open enrollment period, Personal Lines P&C written premium grew 36% YoY, and the broker network expanded from ~65 to ~300 agency partners since 2022 — genuine organic platform growth even as total consolidated revenue shrank due to divestitures [1]. AI Deployment (1/2): Reliance launched a functioning AI agent in July 2026 for secure browser automation in insurance back offices, handling service requests, endorsements, quote pulls, and document retrieval, but no quantified cost savings or revenue contributions have been disclosed three months post-launch [2]. Market Share (0/2): With ~300 agency partners and a handful of owned agencies generating $11M TTM revenue, Reliance remains a negligible participant in the fragmented U.S. insurance distribution market. Product Pipeline (1/2): Management has articulated an AI-native insurance product roadmap and reorganized leadership (new COO, CTO, EVP) around it, but no specific next-generation products with named launch dates or revenue visibility have been disclosed [2]. R&D Intensity (1/1): The June 2026 hiring of a CTO from Coinbase/Capital One and formation of a dedicated AI product development team represents above-average technology investment for a 40-employee company, even as overall headcount and revenue shrink [2].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): CEO Ezra Beyman has articulated a specific thesis that 'insurance, one of the largest and most entrenched industries in the world, was overdue for a fundamental rethinking' via AI — a genuine strategic point of view that differentiates from generic InsurTech language, though unproven by results given ongoing losses and declining revenue [2][3]. Community Impact (0/2): No evidence of charitable programs, foundation activity, or community investment was identified. Employee Retention (0/2): No tenure or turnover data was found; the company has shrunk from ~75 to 40 employees while simultaneously reconstituting its leadership team with a new COO, CTO, and EVP in mid-2026, suggesting organizational instability [2]. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of net insider buying was identified; the company instead raised capital through a $50M equity line of credit and ATM program that dilutes existing shareholders.

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock on available metrics. The stock now clears the IOWN liquidity floor following the May 2026 reverse split recovery — avg_daily_volume of ~1.85M shares at $2.50 implies ~$4.6M in daily dollar volume, above the $1M threshold [4]. However, underlying fundamentals remain deeply distressed: ROE of -123.5% and profit margin of -54.3% both floor at zero contribution, and revenue growth of -31.6% YoY falls well below the -20% floor (score 0.0) as commission income dropped to $2.1M in Q2 2026 from $3.1M a year earlier [1]. Debt-to-equity of 79.3% is slightly above the 70% target (score 0.96), providing the only metric contribution. Forward P/E, PEG, and 5-year revenue CAGR are unavailable for this loss-making micro-cap. Total stockholders' equity of ~$6.65M leaves minimal balance-sheet cushion against continued losses [1].

ai_resilience.label: HIGH RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (4/9): Insurance brokerage and agency distribution faces genuine AI disintermediation risk — AI-native direct carriers, comparison platforms, and large insurers building in-house AI distribution could bypass small independent agency roll-ups like Reliance entirely. The company is proactively defending by building its own AI tools (the July 2026 AI agent, new AI product team) rather than waiting to be disrupted, but with only $2.1M in quarterly commission income and ongoing losses, execution risk is extreme and the outcome uncertain [1][2]. AI Opportunity (0/1): While Reliance has launched an AI agent and reorganized leadership around an AI-native strategy, no specific AI-attributable revenue figures or efficiency gains have been quantified in financial disclosures.

infinite_game.summary: Reliance Global Group is a distressed micro-cap attempting a genuine strategic pivot toward AI-native insurance distribution, but the pivot is happening under severe financial duress — a reverse stock split, dilutive equity financing, shrinking revenue from $14M to $11M over two years, and persistent losses. Sinek would note that a Just Cause tested only under existential financial pressure, with no track record of consistency, cannot yet be distinguished from a survival pivot rather than a purpose-driven transformation.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): CEO Ezra Beyman's stated belief that insurance 'was overdue for a fundamental rethinking' through AI is a specific point of view, but it remains unproven — the company has not demonstrated sustained execution, and the pivot coincides with declining revenue, net losses, and a forced reverse stock split, making it difficult to distinguish genuine cause from necessity [2][3].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Investing in new senior technology leadership (a Coinbase/Capital One CTO) and launching a functioning AI agent product while the company posts net losses and faces dilutive financing shows willingness to invest in long-term capability during financial distress [2]. It remains ambiguous whether this reflects principled long-term conviction or a pivot necessary to justify the company's continued Nasdaq listing and existence.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): No positive culture or retention evidence was found. The workforce shrank from ~75 to ~40 employees while simultaneously reconstituting leadership with a new COO, CTO, and EVP in quick succession — an organization still being rebuilt around a new strategy rather than one with established internal trust or stability [2].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Reliance has been actively divesting non-core insurance agencies while redirecting the business toward an 'AI backbone' for its acquisition roll-up and AI-native insurance products, and formed EZRA International Group in January 2026 to acquire Israeli tech companies — a real, ongoing strategic pivot away from the legacy agency-acquisition model [1][2]. The pivot's success is unproven and is occurring under financial pressure rather than from a position of strength.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No evidence was found of Reliance publicly framing competitors as worthy rivals or a source of self-improvement motivation; the company's competitive language focuses on being 'the first AI-native' insurer rather than learning from existing players.

investment_thesis: Reliance Global Group is a speculative micro-cap attempting to reposition itself as an AI-native InsurTech platform. The July 2026 launch of a functioning AI agent for insurance back-office automation, combined with the hiring of a CTO from Coinbase and Capital One and a newly formed AI product team, gives the company a credible (if unproven) technology story [2]. Underlying organic metrics at RELI Exchange remain positive — health policies written up 72% YoY and P&C premium up 36% YoY during the last enrollment cycle, with the broker network nearly quintupling to ~300 agency partners since 2022 — suggesting the core distribution platform has real product-market traction even as the consolidated entity shrinks to $11M TTM revenue [1]. The stock has recovered from post-split lows to $2.50, and daily dollar volume of ~$4.6M now clears IOWN's $1M liquidity floor.
thesis_continued: The bear case dominates. Consolidated commission income fell 31.7% YoY to $2.1M in Q2 2026 with a $2.0M net loss against just $6.65M of stockholders' equity, leaving virtually no balance-sheet cushion [1]. The company has shrunk from 75 to 40 employees, revenue has declined from $14.1M in 2024 to $11.0M TTM, and the $4.2M market cap reflects the market's view that this is effectively a pre-revenue turnaround story [4]. The newly formed EZRA International Group division to acquire Israeli tech companies adds strategic complexity and potential capital drain to a company that can barely fund its existing operations. With no dividend, no insider buying, no meaningful market share, and persistent losses consuming a thin equity base, Reliance remains a high-risk speculative position that does not meet IOWN's bar for capital allocation regardless of the genuine AI narrative.
key_catalysts: Continued scaling of RELI Exchange organic metrics (72% YoY health policy growth, 36% YoY P&C premium growth, ~300 agency partners) into a larger share of consolidated revenue as non-core agency divestitures roll off the YoY comparison base [1]

Successful monetization of the AI agent and AI-native insurance product roadmap under the new CTO/COO leadership team, potentially improving margins and differentiating Reliance from other small agency roll-ups [2]
Stabilization of the share price and Nasdaq compliance following the May 2026 reverse split, with the stock now trading at $2.50 versus the $1.00 minimum bid requirement
key_risks: Persistent net losses ($2.0M in Q2 2026 alone) against a thin equity base (~$6.65M) leave minimal room for execution missteps in the AI pivot before additional dilutive or distressed financing becomes necessary [1]

Ongoing dilution risk from the $50M equity line of credit and ATM program could substantially increase share count and further pressure per-share economics even if the underlying AI strategy succeeds [3]

The workforce has shrunk to approximately 40 employees — a skeleton crew attempting to simultaneously operate existing insurance businesses, develop AI products, and pursue international tech acquisitions, creating severe execution bandwidth risk [4]
